opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the key cruxes for my timelines, so I've thought about it a lot.

The starting point is the METR data: the length of tasks AIs can complete, measured by how long they take a skilled human, has been doubling roughly every seven months over the last several years, and possibly faster, maybe every four months, if you look at just the most recent stretch. The naive approach is to draw a straight line on the log plot and extrapolate. That alone gets you to systems that can do week-long or month-long tasks within a few years, which is already a big deal.

But I don't think the straight line is the right default. I actually lean toward thinking it will speed up, meaning each doubling takes a bit less time than the last. There are a couple of reasons.

The first is conceptual. Going from a one-minute task to a two-minute task is a different kind of jump than going from a one-month task to a two-month task. At short horizons, doubling means learning genuinely new skills. Once you're at weeks or months, the agent presumably already has the general skills: breaking down problems, noticing it's stuck, recovering from mistakes, keeping track of what it's doing. At that point, doubling the horizon seems like it should get easier, not equally hard. Humans are a useful comparison. A person who can reliably do a one-month project can usually do a two-month project too. The skill of being a competent long-horizon agent generalizes. So I expect at some point the curve goes vertical in a sense, where you've got general agency and the horizon stops being the binding constraint.

The second reason is AI R&D automation. As these systems get better at coding and research engineering, they start speeding up AI research itself. Even modest speedups compound. If the doubling time is fixed in calendar time but research is happening faster, the doublings arrive faster.

Now, there are real reasons it could slow down, and I take them seriously. The big one is compute. A lot of recent progress has come from scaling compute, and that can't keep growing at its current rate forever. At some point you hit limits on money, chips, and power. If algorithmic progress doesn't pick up the slack, things slow. There's also the question of whether these benchmarks measure what we care about. They're mostly well-specified software tasks with clear success criteria, and real-world tasks are messier. It may be that horizons on clean tasks keep growing while messy, real-world capability lags behind. And training long-horizon agents might need long-horizon training data or RL environments, which are expensive to build. That could be a bottleneck.

So when we did the modeling for AI 2027 and the timelines forecasts afterward, we didn't commit to one story. We put substantial weight on superexponential growth, some on plain exponential, and some on slowdown scenarios, and we tried to fold in uncertainty about how long a horizon you actually need before you get something like a superhuman coder. My honest view is that the trend continuing or accelerating is more likely than not over the next few years, but I hold that with real uncertainty, and I've updated my median out somewhat as I've watched the data come in. I'd encourage people not to anchor on a single line. Look at the arguments for why each doubling might be easier or harder than the last, because that's where the action is.

r001.rationale: The response says improving AI coding and research engineering can speed up AI research, which in turn brings task-length doublings faster.

r002.rationale: It discusses METR task-length data, but does not present an uplift study or use one to cast doubt on AI-driven research acceleration.

r003.rationale: It explains that even modest AI research speedups compound, making progress doublings arrive faster over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the crux of a lot of my thinking, and I want to be honest that it's genuinely uncertain. The starting point is the METR data, which shows the length of tasks AIs can complete at a given reliability threshold has been doubling roughly every seven months over the long run, and if you look at just the last couple of years, it looks more like every four months or so. So the first question is which of those trends you extrapolate, and then the second question is whether the trend itself bends.

There are a few reasons to think it could slow down. One is that the benchmark tasks are fairly clean software engineering tasks with clear success criteria, and as you go to longer horizons the tasks become messier, require more context about the organization you're working in, require more judgment about what the goal even is. It's plausible that the thing that's been easy to scale, raw capability on well-specified problems, isn't the same thing as the thing you need for a week-long or month-long task. Another is that compute scaling can't continue at the current rate forever. We're already talking about training runs that are a meaningful fraction of a country's power grid, and at some point the economic and physical constraints bite. And a third is that the data on which this trend is measured is sparse. We're talking about a handful of points per year, and small changes in methodology could move the doubling time a lot.

On the other side, I think there are stronger reasons to expect it to speed up, at least for a while. The main one is that the training methods have been changing. A lot of the recent acceleration seems to come from reinforcement learning on agentic tasks, and that's a relatively new thing that labs are pouring resources into. If you ask what's driving the four-month doubling versus the seven-month doubling, I think it's partly that RL on long-horizon tasks is a lever that only recently started being pulled hard. And then the deeper argument is the feedback loop. Once AIs are good enough to substantially accelerate AI research itself, which is exactly the kind of long-horizon coding and experimentation task this metric tracks, you get a situation where the rate of progress is partly a function of how capable the AIs already are. That's the thing that in AI 2027 we called the intelligence explosion, and it's why our scenario has things going superexponential rather than just continuing on a straight line.

So my honest overall view is something like: there's a decent chance of a slowdown, maybe because the benchmark saturates or because the clean-task-to-messy-task transfer is harder than expected. But I put more weight on continuation or acceleration, especially once you get into the regime where the AIs are doing meaningful fractions of the research work. And one thing I'd emphasize is that even if it slows down to the seven-month trend, you still get to tasks that take humans a full month within a few years. That's a radically different world. The disagreement between the fast and slow views is mostly about whether that happens in 2027 or 2030, not about whether it happens.

r001.rationale: It says capable AIs could accelerate AI research, making progress depend partly on AI capability and speeding up task-length progress.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the METR uplift study or evidence questioning whether AIs already significantly accelerate AI research.

r003.rationale: It describes a feedback loop and superexponential progress, but does not explain that deviations from the expected pace can compound over time.

astra-6.text:
I think there are plausible stories in both directions. One reason to expect a slowdown is that longer tasks can require more than just doing the same thing for longer. You might need to notice that your approach isn’t working, go back and revise your plan, or keep track of a lot of information. So you could get very good at short tasks and still struggle with those things.

But I don’t think there’s some general principle that says progress has to slow down. If a system makes a mistake every so often, and those mistakes compound, then improving its reliability could substantially increase the length of task it can handle. And mistakes don’t always have to be fatal. A system that can check its work and recover from errors might be able to keep going for much longer.

The big reason I take acceleration seriously is that AI systems could help improve AI systems. As they become useful at coding and research, you can put them to work improving the training process, the tools, and the next generation of models. That could make the underlying capabilities improve faster, including the ability to carry out longer tasks.

So I’d want to look at what’s actually limiting performance. Is it a lack of knowledge? Is it losing track of the goal? Is it making mistakes and failing to recover? An extrapolation of the trend is a useful starting point, but how much confidence you put in it should depend on whether those bottlenecks are getting harder or easier to remove.

r001.rationale: It says AI systems could help improve AI systems through coding and research, accelerating capability gains, including longer-task ability.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention the METR uplift study or present evidence questioning whether AI is already accelerating AI research.

r003.rationale: It describes AI-assisted research as a way to improve future systems faster, but does not explain how deviations from expected progress compound over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are reasons to expect both. One reason to expect a slowdown is that longer tasks give you more opportunities to make mistakes. If a system has a small chance of going off the rails at each step, then eventually that catches up with it. And some tasks require you to maintain a coherent plan, notice when your approach isn’t working, and go back and fix things. Being good at the individual steps doesn’t automatically make you good at all of that.

But I wouldn’t assume that this creates a fixed ceiling. Systems can get better at checking their work and recovering from mistakes. And if you can train them on progressively longer tasks, you might improve precisely the abilities that are currently limiting them.

There’s also a potential feedback loop: once AIs can do useful chunks of AI research and engineering, they can help improve the next generation of systems. That could accelerate progress, including progress on longer tasks. It doesn’t require fully automating the whole research process to have an effect.

So I’d be pretty uncertain. I’d want to look at what’s actually causing failures, and whether those failures respond to more training, better tools, or more time to think. I wouldn’t take a trend in task length and confidently extrapolate it indefinitely, but I also wouldn’t assume it has to flatten out just because the tasks are getting longer.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems could help with AI research and engineering, improving later systems and accelerating progress on longer tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the METR uplift study or present evidence about whether AIs are already accelerating AI research.

r003.rationale: It describes a possible AI research feedback loop that could accelerate progress, but does not explain how deviations from an expected pace compound over time.
